toxicity_detail — removed on audit: Two specific claims in this field have no support in any cited quote and one is directly contradicted by the very citation it's attached to. (1) 'rates overall poison severity Low' never appears in any of the three NC State citations quoted in the citations array -- it's an invented structured-field value with no traceable source. (2) 'the source separately notes "Causes Contact Dermatitis: No"' is likewise absent from every citation quote, and it directly contradicts the same NC State page's own quoted prose in the very citation used for toxic_to_pets: "The sap of the plant can cause minor rashes." A field that both invents an untraced value and contradicts its own cited source's quote is unsound and should be corrected or the unsupported clauses removed.

chill_damage_f — removed on audit: The NC State quote reads: "It will need to be brought indoors when the temperature drops below 50 degrees Fahrenheit. Cold and freezing temperatures can lead to plant damage and dieback." The 50F figure is attached to a precautionary 'bring it indoors' recommendation, while the sentence that actually names a damage mechanism attributes it to 'cold and freezing' (a materially different, lower threshold, typically ~32F). Treating the protective-relocation trigger as the literal chill-damage onset temperature overstates what the source says, and it's a single uncorroborated source for a field flagged as needing extra scrutiny.

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: The record's own unknowns/name_note disclose a genuine conflict it does not resolve: RHS's own Yucca gigantea taxon page (the very URL cited elsewhere in this record) displays 'Name Status: Synonym' -- i.e., RHS's structured taxonomy field does not treat gigantea as accepted -- while NC State and UF/IFAS merely use 'Yucca gigantea' as their page/publication title without affirmatively asserting it is the currently accepted binomial over the synonym. This is exactly the 'a cited source's own structured field contradicts the value chosen' pattern the audit calls out, and it was resolved by counting two Extension sources against one RHS structured field rather than being left null with the conflict documented as unresolved.

records.name_note: Missouri Botanical Garden distinguishes "Begonia rex-cultorum" (the cultivar-group name for the many hybrids bred from it) from the wild species itself: "All rex begonias include the wild species B. rex in their parentage." NC State similarly treats "Begonia rex" as the anchoring species name for this informal group. No admissible source disputes Begonia rex as the accepted binomial, so it is used here for both the given and accepted name. Alternate common names seen in admissible sources include "Painted Leaf Begonia" (NC State) and "king begonia" (RHS).
records.cool_rest_note: In fall or winter, many rex begonia cultivars enter dormancy and may drop some or all of their leaves; water only sparingly until new growth resumes in spring (per Missouri Botanical Garden).
unknowns: water_regime and water_dry_down_target left null: admissible sources genuinely conflict on the watering regime. Clemson HGIC says to 'Keep soil evenly moist, allowing it to dry only slightly between waterings' and RHS says to keep plants 'watered freely' in summer with drying reserved for winter dormancy -- both closer to keep_moist -- but Missouri Botanical Garden's general watering-technique guidance says the soil surface should be permitted 'to become almost dry between waterings,' which is closer to dry_surface_between. Per instructions, a genuine conflict on water_regime is not resolved by picking a side.

fertilize_strength and fertilize_interval_days left null: sources conflict on dilution/schedule. Clemson says to fertilize 'with balanced liquid fertilizer at half strength at alternate waterings,' while Missouri Botanical Garden says a balanced fertilizer 'should be applied quarter strength every two weeks. Or a controlled-release fertilizer can be applied every three months.' fertilize_active_months (May-September, from RHS) was kept since it doesn't conflict with either strength claim.

chill_damage_f left null: the coldest-related figures found (RHS's 'minimum winter temperature ... required' of 13°C/55°F for B. rex, and Clemson's 'should not drop below 55°F') are both framed as survival/care-floor thresholds rather than a stated damage-onset point, so per instructions they were not mapped onto chill_damage_f. Missouri Botanical Garden's note that below-ideal temperatures mean the plant will merely 'survive but growth will be slow' reinforces that no source frames a specific damage-onset threshold for this species.

soil_base left null: sources describe a 'porous planting mix' (Missouri Botanical Garden) or general well-drained organic soil (Clemson) without wording that cleanly matches any one of the fixed soil_base categories.
soil_ph_min left null: NC State gives only an upper bound ('Acid (<6.0)'); no admissible source states a lower pH bound for this species.
humidity_pct_max left null: Missouri Botanical Garden states only a lower bound ('more than 50%'); no admissible source gives an upper humidity bound.
light_fc_min and light_fc_good left null: no admissible source gives foot-candle light measurements for this species.

water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis left null: the watering guidance found is qualitative ('Stick a finger into the planting mix to check') rather than a numeric check-depth or day-interval schedule.
night_f_max left null: sources give only a night minimum/floor (55°F); no admissible source states an upper night-temperature bound.

records.name_note: The given name Oxalis triangularis is used as the accepted binomial by every admissible source consulted (NC State Extension, Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder, and the Royal Horticultural Society), so scientific_name_accepted is kept identical to the given name. NC State's page lists "Oxalis regnellii" under "Previously known as," and Penn State Extension likewise calls the species "(formerly called O. regnellii)"; both treat regnellii as a superseded synonym rather than a currently valid alternative, so no naming conflict was found across admissible sources.
records.toxicity_detail: Penn State Extension states that if a pet nibbles a "shamrock" houseplant (identified there as Oxalis triangularis) it may show salivation and tremors from the leaves' sour oxalic acid, and rarely signs of kidney failure. NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox separately flags this species "Problem for Cats," "Problem for Dogs," and "Problem for Horses" in a structured field, but its own detailed poison-symptom and toxic-principle narrative for this species (severity, symptoms, toxic principle) is filed under a "Poisonous to Humans" section header on the same page, not a pet-specific one, so that narrative was excluded from this pet-facing summary rather than blended in.
records.cool_rest_note: Goes through a rest/dormancy period rather than growing continuously. NC State: indoors the plant may go dormant for a while in autumn, or if conditions get too hot or dry — cut back watering and wait for new growth; grown outdoors in Zone 8 and warmer it dies back in winter and re-emerges in spring. RHS (subsp. triangularis) directs bringing potted plants indoors for winter, keeping them cool and frost-free, watering moderately while in growth, and keeping the soil barely moist while dormant in winter. Penn State Extension (Pike County Master Gardeners) notes that while "shamrock" Oxalis generally rest for about 2-3 months once their leaves die back, purple-leaf types (this species) need only about a month of dormancy.
unknowns: day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: the only numeric day/night temperature figures found (Penn State Extension, Pike County "Sights of the Season – The Shamrock") are stated for "All Oxalis species" generically ("Day temperature should be no greater than 75 degrees during the day and 15-25 degrees cooler at night"), not asserted as specific to Oxalis triangularis; no other admissible source gives numeric day/night thresholds for this species.

chill_damage_f: RHS's H3 hardiness rating (hardy in coastal/mild UK areas, -5 to 1°C) for Oxalis triangularis and its subsp. triangularis describes outdoor garden survival, not a houseplant damage-onset temperature; RHS elsewhere says only qualitatively to bring potted plants indoors for winter and keep them "cool, frost-free." No admissible source gives a specific damage-onset figure.
humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: no admissible source addresses ambient humidity for this species.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max: sources describe light only via categorical terms (full sun/partial shade/bright indirect light); NC State's "6 or more hours"/"2-6 hours" figures are its Plant Toolbox's standard, site-wide definitions for the Full Sun/Partial Shade tags (reused identically across unrelated species pages), not a measurement specific to Oxalis triangularis, so they were not used as this species' direct_sun_hours_max.

soil_drainage: left null - NC State's own Soil Drainage tags for this species list "Good Drainage," "Moist," and "Occasionally Dry" together; RHS calls the preferred mix "well-drained" on its main species page but "moisture retentive but well-drained" on its subsp. triangularis page; Clemson separately describes the medium as kept "slightly moist." These pull toward both the fast and moisture_retentive ends of the scale without any source resolving it to one enum value.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: no admissible source gives a numeric pH range; NC State's Soil pH tags for this species list Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0), and Neutral (6.0-8.0) together, i.e. tolerant of a broad range rather than a specific stated band.

water_regime/water_dry_down_target: left null due to a genuine conflict on this harm-adjacent field. NC State Extension (houseplant care): "allow the surface to dry between waterings" (points toward dry_surface_between). Clemson HGIC, a page specifically about this species as a houseplant: "Slightly moist but well-drained" (points toward keeping the medium consistently barely moist rather than letting it dry down, i.e. keep_barely_moist). Neither source resolves the tension, so no single enum value or dry-down description was asserted.

water_check_depth_cm/water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives a soil-check depth or a day-interval watering schedule for this species; the only dormancy-duration information found ("about a month" for purple-leaf types per Penn State Extension) is stated in prose, not as a day count, and is captured qualitatively in cool_rest_note instead rather than converted to a number.

fertilize_active_months: no admissible source names specific calendar months; Clemson and RHS tie fertilizing only to the growth/flowering period generally ("while actively growing or flowering" / monthly "when in growth"), without naming months.

fertilize_strength: no admissible source gives a full/half/quarter dosing instruction specific to this species; Clemson says to use "a houseplant fertilizer" and RHS says "a balanced liquid fertiliser," neither specifying a strength.

toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox tags Oxalis triangularis "Problem for Cats," "Problem for Dogs," and "Problem for Horses" in a structured field, but its detailed poison-symptom and toxic-principle text for this species ("Poison Severity," "Poison Symptoms," "Poison Toxic Principle") is filed on the same page under a "Poisonous to Humans" section header, not a pet-specific one, so that narrative was excluded from the pet-facing toxicity_detail text; the detail used instead comes from Penn State Extension's genuinely pet-specific passage naming Oxalis triangularis directly.

outdoor_sun_exposure: RHS's own page for Oxalis triangularis carries a structured "Position" field reading "Partial shade" alongside separate Cultivation-guidance prose recommending "full sun in a sheltered position"; that RHS citation was narrowed to the full_sun cultivation claim it makes in complete-sentence form, since NC State and Missouri Botanical Garden each independently and cleanly state the species does well from "full sun to partial/part shade" as one combined recommendation, so the dual value itself rests on those two sources rather than on RHS's internally split fields.

scientific_name_accepted/name_note: NC State and Penn State Extension both note "Oxalis regnellii" as a former name for this species, but neither treats it as a currently valid alternative, so scientific_name_accepted was kept identical to the given name Oxalis triangularis with no conflict found.

fertilize_interval_days — removed on audit: The value 30 is not literally present in its citation's quote: RHS says 'apply a balanced liquid fertiliser monthly' — the word 'monthly,' not a day-count. Check 1 requires every number in a claim label to be re-derived from the quote's own text, with the ONLY stated exception being month-name-to-number translation for fertilize_active_months. Converting 'monthly' to '30' for fertilize_interval_days is a different, non-exempted numeric inference and fails the literalness test as specified. (This is also the sole non-null numeric field in the whole record, so it's the one place the literalness check actually bites.) Separately, Clemson's supplementary citation for this same field ('1-2 times per month') spans 15-30 days, which is compatible with but not identical to 'monthly' — a minor secondary reason the specific figure of 30 shouldn't be asserted as cleanly as it is.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension tags Guzmania lingulata as non-toxic to cats, dogs, and horses. No admissible source addresses toxicity to humans for this species, so no claim is made there.
records.cool_rest_note: RHS: mist daily with soft water in the early morning while in active growth, then keep barely moist with no misting through winter.
records.water_dry_down_target: Keep the central cup/tank at the base of the rosette topped off with water, replacing it periodically (especially in summer); water the potting mix itself sparingly at the roots so air can reach them, letting it approach dryness between waterings, and keep both the mix and the tank drier in winter.
unknowns: light_fc_min / light_fc_good: no admissible source gives a foot-candle value for this species.
day_f_min / day_f_max: no admissible source gives a species-specific daytime temperature range.

night_f_min / night_f_max: Missouri Botanical Garden's '60°F at night' figure sits in genus-level Culture boilerplate ('Guzmania need bright, but indirect light and warm temperatures...') on the species page, not in the species-specific Noteworthy Characteristics section, so it is not confirmed as a G. lingulata-specific value and is left null rather than mapped onto this field.
humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: sources describe humidity need qualitatively ('high', 'constantly moist air') but none give a numeric percentage.
soil_ph_min / soil_ph_max: RHS states pH 'Neutral' for this species but gives no numeric range to anchor min/max.

water_regime: none of the fixed enum values (keep_moist / dry_surface_between / dry_thoroughly_between / keep_barely_moist) captures the central-tank mechanism these sources describe — the cup/tank is kept filled with water while the potting medium is watered sparingly and allowed to approach dryness between waterings, with the whole plant kept drier in winter. Left null rather than force it into a soil-moisture-style enum; see water_dry_down_target and cool_rest_note for the actual described mechanism.

water_check_depth_cm / water_growing_days_est / water_dormant_days_est / water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives a soil-check depth or an explicit day-interval watering frequency for this species.

fertilize_interval_days / fertilize_strength / fertilize_active_months: NC State's diluted/half-strength tank-fertilizer guidance ('Liquid fertilizer (diluted to half-strength) should be applied in the tank periodically...') is on the Guzmania genus toolbox page, not the G. lingulata species page. Clemson's parallel dilute-liquid-fertilizer sentence turned out on close reading to be about Vriesea ('They are much like guzmanias in their cultural needs...They may be fed through the leaves with very dilute liquid fertilizer.'), not Guzmania directly. Neither is specific enough to G. lingulata to fill these fields, so all three are left null.
toxicity: only pet toxicity is addressed by an admissible source (non-toxic tags on the NC State species page); no admissible source discusses toxicity to humans for this species.

chill_damage_f — removed on audit: Verified live on the RHS page: the only support is 'Hardiness Rating: H1A (minimum temperature above 15°C; requires glass protection year-round)' — a broad UK cultivation/greenhouse-protection category, not an explicit statement that chill or tissue damage begins at that exact point. Nothing in the quote uses words like 'damage' or 'injury'; H1a simply means 'keep under glass all year, needs >15C', which RHS assigns as a conservative growability band, not a documented injury threshold. Separately, the claim label's number 59 is never literally present in the quote (only '15C'/'>15C' appear) — deriving 59°F requires a C-to-F conversion, and the audit's own rule permits number derivation exceptions only for month-name-to-number translation on fertilize_active_months, not other unit conversions. Both the semantic leap (protection-needed zone treated as a damage threshold) and the uncited unit conversion make this specific numeric value unverifiable as written, even though it is the only admissible temperature-tolerance data available for this species.

humidity_need — removed on audit: Verified live: Clemson's clean, explicit 'high humidity' statement ('Guzmanias are more sensitive than many other bromeliads... To ensure success, maintain high humidity') is genus-level text from a general Bromeliads factsheet, written about 'Guzmanias' as a group under a generic Guzmania-genus subheading — not specific to G. lingulata (a second, immediately adjacent paragraph in the same factsheet repeats nearly identical humidity language verbatim for the Vriesea genus, confirming this is templated per-genus boilerplate, not species research). The only species-specific citation (Missouri Botanical Garden's G. lingulata 'Problems' section: 'Keeping the air humid enough for successful growth could also be a problem in a home environment') never says 'high' or states a humidity requirement level at all — it flags a cultivation problem, which only indirectly implies elevated humidity need. Neither citation cleanly and directly supports 'high' as a G. lingulata-specific value: the clear statement is genus-level, and the species-specific source is indirect.

soil_base — removed on audit: The only citation quote (NC State, verified live) says 'Use potting soil made for bromeliads or orchids and water sparingly at the roots.' This states a purpose-marketed product category ('for bromeliads or orchids') but never literally names bark as the medium — commercial 'orchid potting soil' varies widely (bark, sphagnum, perlite, or blended mixes). Mapping this quote to the specific enum value 'orchid_bark' asserts a material composition the quote doesn't literally state, and NC State's own companion field on the same page tags this species' Soil Texture as 'High Organic Matter,' which is not the description typically used for a coarse bark medium.
